description: As media outlets report on the probability of the US attacking Iran, many are instead turning to prediction markets to find out, and bet, on the odds.  . Al Jazeera's @Linh N. explains the rise in betting on war. #digitaldilemma
_transcript: How much would you bet that the U.S. will attack Iran by the end of February? Or next month? Or the end of this year? While media outlets have been reporting on the U.S. military buildup in the Middle East, people have been turning to prediction markets to find out the odds of anything happening. On platforms like PolyMarket, millions of dollars are already pouring into the probability of this strike happening. Supporters of these platforms describe them as valuable sources of information that harness the wisdom of the crowd. After all, PolyMarket correctly predicted a win by Donald Trump in the 2024 U.S. presidential election before the polls did. But critics of prediction markets say they dehumanize conflict, since these are real-world events with human costs. When Israel, with the help of the U.S., attacked Iran in June 2025, hundreds of people were killed and thousands were injured during 12 days of war. But even before a single bomb was dropped, PolyMarket users were already making bets on when it would happen. One market predicted that Israel would hit Iranian oil infrastructures in June with a probability greater than 99%. Right now, PolyMarket and Caoshi are the two biggest in this space, and they're growing fast, but with differences. Caoshi is a regulated U.S. exchange and trades in U.S. dollars. It has banned bets involving war or assassination. PolyMarket, on the other hand, allows these sorts of bets and trades in cryptocurrency. It runs on the blockchain and its users are often anonymous. People bet on all sorts of future events on these platforms. There's the more benign, like the date of Taylor Swift's wedding, to the geopolitical, like the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. One anonymous user made $400,000 on PolyMarket by betting Maduro would be out by the end of January, which raised some red flags about potential insider trading. The fallout from prediction markets doesn't end there. In one instance, Israel's internal security agency arrested and charged several people suspected of using classified military information on PolyMarket, although the agency did not clarify which particular bets allegedly took place on the platform. Another concern with sites like PolyMarket is whether they amount to gambling or are seen as financial markets. The answer varies depending on the country's regulatory body. Countries like the U.K., France and Singapore have blocked PolyMarket and classified it as gambling. In the U.S., opinion varies state to state, and there's at least 20 federal lawsuits against companies like Caoshi and PolyMarket. But the founders of these platforms disagree. The CEO of PolyMarket, Shane Copland, said that unlike a betting site where you make a bet and it's against the house, on PolyMarket you own a share. For Copland, prediction markets operate more like financial forecasting tools. They're information sources that could replace polls, pundits and media institutions. And many major news outlets have already signed partnerships with these platforms to gain access to their prediction data. But of course, there's a difference between predicting sports and betting on a wall, and the ethical concerns that come with that. So, do these platforms provide clarity, or do they turn human suffering into financial gain? These questions will become more pressing as geopolitical bets continue to rise.

Elections are a sacred function of democracy and can have lasting consequences. So gambling on them feels like it's on the same level of morbidity as betting when your dog is going to die, or doing a parlay on which two of your wife's friends will divorce first. But this country has a long history of betting on elections, going back to the early 1800s. As these papers by Paul Rode and Coleman Strumpf explain, the tradition really intensified during the Jacksonian era, with up to $6 million being wagered in New York during the 1844 presidential election between Henry Clay and James Polk. The practice reached another peak starting in the 1880s and 1890s and lasting until the 1910s, with about $10 million in political bets wagered in New York in 1916. Newspapers regularly reported on the market odds for election bets, which allowed everyday people to keep up with how presidential races were going. In a time before reliable scientific polling, these gambling odds were the closest to consistent and reliable sources that many people had on which way the election might swing. Interestingly, for most people during this era, betting wasn't seen as a way to make money as much as it was just another way to support a candidate that you were going to vote for anyway, or a way to back your beliefs. Many of these bets didn't even involve money. Freak bets, as Rode and Strumpf call them, involved wild dares that you'd have to do if your candidate lost, like pushing your friend around in a wheelbarrow, or whatever kinky stuff this guy is doing. One estimate stated that there were half a million of these freak bets in the election of 1900 alone. And hey, let's bring that back instead of gambling money on the outcome. Other factors, like the suppression of illegal gambling and the legalization of horse racing, also drew people away from election betting. Yep, people stopped betting on presidential elections once they realized it was much easier and quicker to just bet on horses instead. So what brought the practice back? Well, the way that people can bet on elections now is through what's known as event contracts, which are agreements to buy or sell a commodity asset for a predetermined price at a certain point in the future, dependent on the outcome of a specific event. Basically, you buy in on a certain position, which is either yes or no to whether that event will happen, and if you're right, you receive money. These types of contracts are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which tried to prevent the trading of event contracts tied to the outcomes of elections by saying they were classified as election gambling. However, the District Court found that there was not sufficient evidence that this was gambling, and the Appeals Court agreed, allowing Kolschi to continue letting people place bets on elections. So there you have it. It's not gambling, it's just placing money on a discrete outcome that you have no control over in which you will receive more money than you put in. Very different from gambling. But the proliferation of election betting raises another problem, as more and more news outlets and even presidential candidates start using betting odds as evidence of who will win the election, there comes the question, how accurate are these odds compared to polling? I mean, why does 538 show Kamala Harris having a 54% chance of winning, and Kolschi show Trump having a 57% chance? If we look at how Kolschi determines their odds, we can see that the price and probability are assigned by continually assessing the collective sentiment of its users regarding the likelihood of an event resulting in a yes or no. Sites like Kolschi don't use external polling data to assess the likelihood of a Trump or Harris victory, and instead rely solely on the betting behavior of their users to determine who is more likely to win. This can make these sites subject to self-selection bias, where the odds represent the sentiment of people who choose to bet on elections rather than the sentiments of a randomized group of voters. For instance, according to Wired, three quarters of traffic to the betting site Polly Market comes from men, so that site's odds wouldn't be representative of the American electorate as a whole. And this might be fine if all of these bettors were trading rationally and betting solely on external information. But if election bets remain as a way to back one's beliefs, then these odds just represent the voting behavior of a non-representative section of voters. But at the end of the day, the biggest concern with election betting isn't how accurate it can be, but the danger it could pose to our democracy. In a system where the assumed odds of victory for a candidate are solely determined by the amount of money wagered on them, there's the possibility of large bets placed on certain candidates with the intent to change odds in their favor. For instance, in 1892, Republican campaign managers purposely bet large amounts at more favorable odds for their own candidate, leading newspapers the next day to report that that candidate was performing better in the polls than he actually was. More recently, in 2012, one single bettor on the site Intrade accounted for one-third of the total money placed on Mitt Romney to win the presidential election in the two weeks leading up to the election, single-handedly pushing up his odds of victory on the site. Market manipulation like this could have tangible effects on the election, influencing campaign morale, fundraising, and even voter turnout. description: Luana Lopes Lara, co-founder and COO of Kalshi, discusses how she and her co-founder set out to build something fundamentally different: a platform where people trade on real-world outcomes, not stocks. Listen to the full interview on the CNBC Changemakers and Power Players podcast at the #linkinbio or the link on screen. #CNBC
_transcript: What is the origin of Calshi? What was the original idea? It really started when me and my co-founder, we were working on Wall Street. And what we learned at the time is that most trading happens when you have some view about the future and then you try to put it in the markets, but there isn't a very good way to do it. So an example, for example, is when Brexit was happening in 2016, a lot of people were trying to get exposure to it, but there wasn't a good way. You try to build a portfolio of maybe shorting the pound, go long some European stocks, but there wasn't a direct way to just get exposure about what was going to happen. And we saw the behavior happen a lot, a lot of times. So we saw it again when the Trump 2016 election, that there wasn't a way to really get exposure to it. So people were trying to short the S&P and try to find a play in the markets. But what we wanted to do from that moment on was we wanna create an exchange where people can trade directly on what's gonna happen in the future and just hold exposure, just hold a share of what's going to happen in the future. And of course, the big question at the time, the big problem was how do we make this in a legal way? Because it was illegal in the US. So we went for a four-year regulatory journey to convince the regulators that these markets are good, that they should be regulated and legal in the US for us to be able to launch and go from there. And yeah, in the past two years, since we started listing the election markets, it started growing so much and it's been a blessing.

_transcript: Is insider trading always bad? A network of linked accounts made almost a million dollars in the past two years betting on the timing of American and Israeli strikes on Iran. The accounts placed large bets on Polymarket, a prediction market, with a nearly perfect record of success, implying that the people behind them had advanced knowledge of war plans. Prediction market platforms have grown exponentially in recent years. These sites let you bet on pretty much anything. Most trading is on sports or big elections. But the outcomes of some markets are entirely, well, predictable, if you already know the answer. Should this type of informed trading be completely banned? In the stock market, trading on material non-public information is rightly illegal in most countries. These markets exist so that the public can invest their savings into companies. If informed trading were legal, ordinary investors would know they were at a disadvantage and stay out of the market completely, depriving firms of capital. But futures markets, which now include prediction markets, are different. They were originally built for industry members like wheat farmers to hedge their exposure to market prices, making use of their private knowledge. Because these markets don't have the same capital-raising function as the stock market does, America permits informed trading of futures. And in prediction markets, informed trading arguably offers benefits. Highly informed traders produce more accurate prices on these platforms. And the better prices on these platforms are, the more people know about what's going to happen. And everyone has access to this information, even people who never place a bet. For example, American importers who saw that prediction markets thought the Supreme Court was very likely to throw out Donald Trump's tariffs could have saved themselves a lot of money by delaying shipments from abroad. This doesn't mean that all informed trading in prediction markets is OK. The first exception is when the disclosure of information is harmful rather than helpful. This was the case in Iran. You can see that in the hours before the strike, a flurry of suspicious trades jacked up the price that an attack was imminent. These price surges could have alerted those operations' targets of looming military action against them. Another category requiring regulation is markets where traders can not only bet on outcomes, but also affect whether they happen. Sometimes these cases can be trivial, like someone betting that there'll be a streaker in the Super Bowl and then running onto the field naked themselves. But they can also be deadly serious. PolyMarket recently withdrew a market on the Artemis II crewed moon rocket exploding because it created a financial reward for sabotage. Regulators already require prediction markets to verify users' identities and to maintain market surveillance systems that hunt for suspicious activity. The platforms could make investigators' jobs easier by requiring verification of where money is coming from and where traders work. They could also forge platforms to add disclaimers on markets where some traders might know the outcome in advance so that everyone is aware of the risks. Informed trading in prediction markets leads to better forecasts for everyone. It needs careful regulation, but banning it altogether would be throwing out the baby with the bathwater.
